content:
A pastor opened a recent campaign event for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley with a prayer, asking God to grant the event "integrity and honesty" and to correct the "falsehoods imposed upon the conservative movement."

By North Carolina political standards, such a prayer is not unusual. What was surprising was the person delivering it. According to state government and court records, pastor Daimon L. King is a registered sex offender who has been sentenced to prison twice on charges involving children.

The incident comes two months into a closely watched Senate race whose outcome could determine which party controls the chamber after the November election. It threatens to undermine one of Whatley's core campaign arguments — that his Democratic opponent, former governor Roy Cooper, is soft on crime. It also potentially hands ammunition to Democratic ad campaigns that have long targeted the Republican candidate over his ties to another convicted sex offender who held a Republican Party position.

King did not respond to requests for comment.

Whatley's campaign declined to make him available for an interview. Campaign spokesman DJ Griffin issued a statement saying Whatley did not know King and that the event "was not planned or organized by the Whatley campaign, and the campaign did not invite any guests."

He stressed that King was invited by the "host organization," which he identified as the Craven County Republican Party.

The county party could not be reached for comment.

Whatley led the state and national GOP before running for Senate

Whatley served as chairman of the North Carolina Republican Party beginning in 2019, until 2024, when he was elevated by Trump to chair the Republican National Committee. He later resigned that post at the president's behest to run for the Senate seat.

Chris Cooper, a political science professor at Western Carolina University, said King's prayer and Whatley's ties to another convicted sex offender, former Republican official Harvey L. West Jr., could be especially problematic for the Republican Senate candidate as he works to lock down support from the far-right conservative flank. Cooper is not related to the former governor.

Trump supporters' deep frustration with the government's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case has prompted the president to sign legislation to release related files.

Those documents detail the late sex offender's interactions with prominent figures in politics and business, bringing long-standing suspicions within right-wing circles about the powerful and power structures into broader public discussion.

"The far right has not yet coalesced behind" Whatley, Cooper said, "and this kind of exposure only makes that problem worse."

Pastor prayed at event attended by Whatley and senior Trump administration officials

King, 60, is pastor of New Beginnings Celebration in New Bern, a small coastal town in North Carolina where the event was held on Aug. 28. The pastor has become increasingly active in Republican politics in recent years, positioning himself as a pro-Trump Black conservative, and serves as a precinct chair for the Craven County Republican Party. In sermons posted to YouTube, he has praised Trump, condemned "fake news" and described his message as "the pure, uncut Word of God."

At the event held at the Craven County Republican Party headquarters, Whatley appeared alongside former daytime TV host and current Trump administration Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz.

In a video posted by the Whatley campaign to X, formerly known as Twitter, King can be seen positioning himself in front of the cameras, nodding and giving two thumbs up as Whatley and Oz took turns slamming fraud in the health care system.

"The atmosphere was prayerful and patriotic as we all said the Pledge of Allegiance to the flag of the United States of America!!!" King wrote, adding that he and his church were "all in and standing behind Whatley."

Nearly 30 years ago, King was charged with statutory rape and taking indecent liberties with a 15-year-old student while working as a marching band assistant at a high school in a Raleigh suburb, according to reporting by The News & Observer at the time. State corrections records show that King, then 31, was convicted in 1998 and was paroled after serving nearly five years.

In 2010, he pleaded guilty to having sex with a minor female relative, and state records show he served nearly three years.

Under North Carolina law, King must register as a sex offender for life.

Democrats have hammered Whatley over his ties to another convicted sex offender

Whatley has been dogged since March by his ties to West, who served as a congressional district committee chair for the state GOP while Whatley was chairman.

Records show West served as a small-town police officer before being convicted on five counts of taking indecent liberties with a child and serving six years in prison.

News reports of his conviction in 2012 forced West to resign as an alternate delegate to the Republican National Convention.

According to The Associated Press at the time, West denied committing the offenses and said he had pleaded guilty to avoid the risk of facing decades in prison. He is no longer required to register as a sex offender.

West's conviction resurfaced as a campaign issue earlier this year when Republican activists publicly raised concerns about his continued role in the party. The state GOP has since barred convicted sex offenders from holding party positions.

Democrats have, nonetheless, continued to hammer Whatley over the issue, spending more than $2.3 million on ads featuring a photo of Whatley alongside West.

West says he warned GOP officials about King's conviction

West said in an interview that he had been upfront with party leadership about his past, noting that his main role in the state GOP was elected. He acknowledged that other roles had been appointed while Whatley was chairman.

"I wouldn't say Michael Whatley put me there, but I wasn't removed either," West said.

West said he had worked hard to make amends for his past misdeeds and expressed resignation that his conviction had become a campaign issue.

"I'm just trying to serve people on my own redemptive path. We have a right to be part of the political process. I've been very transparent for these 20 years about who I am and what happened. Not everyone does that," West said.

West also said he was aware of King's conviction record and, when King was being considered for a role in the Republican Party, he warned others in the party against associating with the pastor. "I just said, 'Hey, you all might want to look into that,'" West said.
